result:
The constant is $c = 2/3$. I derived this from the space-barrier construction and recalled, rather than re-derived, that it is the extremal case.

**Extremal construction.** Choose $S_i\subset V_i$ with $|S_i|\approx n/3$ for $i=1,2,3$, so $|S_1|+|S_2|+|S_3|<n$. Take all triples that meet $S=S_1\cup S_2\cup S_3$. Every edge of a perfect matching would need its own vertex of $S$, and a perfect matching has $n$ edges, so none exists.

**Link graph of a vertex outside $S$.** Take $v\in V_1\setminus S_1$. Its link is the bipartite graph on $V_2\cup V_3$ in which $uw$ is an edge exactly when $u\in S_2$ or $w\in S_3$. That is the complete bipartite graph minus a $(2n/3)\times(2n/3)$ block.

**Spectral radius of this link.** Collapse each side into its two parts, of relative sizes $1/3$ and $2/3$. The symmetrized quotient matrix is
$$\begin{pmatrix}1/3 & \sqrt2/3\\ \sqrt2/3 & 0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Its characteristic equation is $\lambda^2-\lambda/3-2/9=0$, and the largest root is $\lambda=2/3$. So $\rho(N_H(v)) = 2n/3$ for these vertices. The other vertices have larger link spectral radius, so the minimum over all vertices is $2n/3$. This shows $c$ cannot be below $2/3$.

**Other barriers.** The divisibility-type constructions have link spectral radius only about $n/2$, which is weaker than the space barrier. I take it from the known result on perfect matchings in 3-partite 3-graphs that the space barrier is the extremal one, which gives the matching sufficiency at $(2/3+\alpha)n$.

ANSWER: 2/3
